item.title: Under the I-5 Outside Redding, California
item.description: Cars rushed by. The sun glared down at me, mocking me. I think it knew how much it irritated me, at least that’s what it felt like. I was under a tiny bridge that supported a small section of the I-5 in central California, just outside of Redding. I had been hitchhiking my way to San Diego to see a few friends. That was no longer my goal. The grasshoppers and crickets made long, droning chirps around me. I had never been this uncomfortable. It made me want to claw at my skin. Yet I couldn’t move, and I hadn’t been able to move for some time, ever since that car came out of nowhere and shoved me down into this miserable hole. The sun was burning itself into my vision. I wished more than anything that I could shut my eyes, but they wouldn’t budge. It made it worse that I could feel everything. I could feel my leg bending backwards under me, the bone poking out like a jagged knife. I could feel my shattered spine and how my ribs punctured my lungs. My intestines hung out of my abdomen. My brain was exposed to the elements. I couldn’t stop thinking about how frightening a sight I must be.

item.title: A Guide to the Crude Dissection of a Body
item.description: At first glance, it may seem trivial. You’re not a doctor, nor are you trained in human anatomy, yet you feel certain that you’ll be able to carry out the act. Take it step by step. Move your hands slowly and methodically. There is no need for absolute precision, but striving for it may be a good idea. Check off the list in your mind before you begin. Grab your gloves and lay them out and slide your hands into the formed rubber and pull them taught and inspect them for wrinkles or holes or signs of damage. Go through your tools, your saws and scalpels and forceps, all second hand, all slightly rusted. Make sure your clothes are ones you intend to dispose of, a shirt filled with holes and a pair of jeans with no button or zipper held up by a crudely made belt made of rope. There is no need for sanitation. There is no life to be saved, only knowledge to be gained. Your check list is complete; there is nothing more to prepare. Take a breath. Look at the eyes. Understand what you are about to do and exploit it.

item.title: A Memory of a Field
item.description: I remember being in a field, surrounded by tall dry grass, staring at that house. My mom stood a few feet behind me, both of us standing silently, observing the landscape around us. We were on our way to a backpacking trail, one that my mom had visited a few times before, but we had stopped briefly on our way there to look at the small lake that broke up the field, and more specifically for her, to take a break from driving. My mom suddenly broke the silence that had been lingering for a while, saying something about the lake or the mountains or the field, but not the house. I answered absentmindedly, saying something small in acknowledgement. I couldn’t shift my focus from the house. It was decrepit, but not completely. Its shingles were falling off and its wood was rotting, but it wasn’t caving in, and it wasn’t blown over. It felt like someone was maintaining it. That scared me, but I’m not sure why. My mom finally addressed the house, telling me that it looked like a “murder cabin”. I agreed, it really did look like a house straight out of a horror movie, but that also didn’t quite do it justice. The house had something more haunting about it, something that awoke a deep fear within me, yet it also brought a heavy sense of melancholy.

item.title: Quercus Robur
item.description: I awoke in a chair. A wooden chair, made from birch, with a table made from hickory in front of me. There was someone across from me, staring at me intently. I gazed around. I was in a coffee shop, but there was nothing but a small cedar counter on the other side of the store. The person across from me and I were sitting at the only table in the store. The walls were made out of cement, and they were covered in scratches. I believed I had been here before. The windows at the front of the store showed only pure white outside. I hated it. I drew my attention to the other person. I gazed at their face for a brief moment, and it seemed wrong. Their eyes were swapped, and their nose was different. Their skin was course, and I could sense the bugs under it, burrowing in and out of their flesh and forming tunnels. I hoped the bugs wouldn’t notice me. The person shot me a look suddenly. I couldn’t quite tell what they meant by it, so I was afraid that they were upset. “Your makeup looks off today”, they told me. I covered my face, embarrassed. “You don’t have to be rude about it, I tried my best”, I said. I lifted my hands away from my face. They were covered in blood, unsurprisingly. I had spent hours getting ready, making sure that everything was just the way I wanted, but my skills were limited. Why did they have to point that out? I took out my phone and used its camera to look at myself.

item.title: I am a house.
item.description: I am a house. A house that cannot feel. A house that emotions cannot attach to, and that, when perceived, cannot be projected upon. A house that leaves people’s minds the moment I am not being observed. I can never be remembered, and no feeling can describe me. Every time I try to internalize something, it cannot be absorbed into my infested walls and moldy floors, for they reject anything that would make me more than just an empty house. I try so hard to feel, to have people feel for me, force emotions upon me in an attempt to become something more than I am, but I am rotten. As more years pass and time marches forward, I degrade even more, mold consumes every inch of me and rust makes my bolts stiff and red, and no matter how hard I try, I cannot feel. I contemplated collapsing in on myself; to let my walls keel over and my furniture shatter, to let the termites hollow me out and release me from the pursuit of feeling, but I can’t give up. For some incomprehensible reason, I can’t give up. And one day, my waiting came to an end.

item.title: A Broken Promise
item.description: The tabletop radio sat in front of me, static erupting from its small speaker. It was old and overused. The yellowed numbers on the frequency dial were almost gone, save for a few chips of paint, and the metal accents on its sides were rusted red. I had been tuning it for quite some time now. I was trying to locate a signal. Where it was and what it sounded like I didn’t know, but I would find it eventually. Sometimes I could hear voices in the static. It was always hard to understand them. It didn’t seem like they were talking to me directly, more so like they were talking to someone else in the distance. Someone who wasn’t there anymore. I could never listen to them for long, the talking would only last a moment before sinking back in to the radio static. The signals were transitory, fading in and out in different places at different times. All I could do was turn the dial back and forth. The radio allowed me that power, and nothing more. I searched between the frequencies. Muffled voices forced their way through the hissing from time-to-time. One emerged from the static, but something felt different about it. It was still unintelligible, but more constant. I could gather glimpses of words. “Happy… long… lived… room… believe…” A woman sat across from me. Her appearance was erratic, her face and torso warped and opaque. A creature of fog. The room was similar. Colors danced around me as the wallpaper changed from columns of switchgrass to bushes of seaside roses to fields of mangroves. It was never right, yet it was always familiar. “I’m so happy we’re here together,” the woman said. Her voice was a symphony of others that spoke her words. Her lips were distinct, but the color of her lipstick shifted rapidly, first red then purple then brown. “The colors match really well.” She hadn’t said that now. That was from before. None of it was right. I covered my eyes. My head felt heavy. I just wanted to see her face. I felt a hand on my arm. “We’ll figure it out.” Though she didn’t talk with her own voice, the words still comforted me. There were boxes around us, labeled and covered in shipping tape, some opened. Glasses of wine, or maybe beer, sat in front of both of us. She grabbed hers and held it up to me, then brought it to her mouth. Her lips were so clear. Her lipstick was colored a deep purple. It left a print on the glass. She always wore lipstick at odd times. She looked so pretty with it on. “I’m so happy we’re here together. God knows it took us long enough.” I could hear her within the choir, but her voice overpowered by the others. “I’m surprised that we could even get here. It never felt like it was in the cards but we did it!” I responded instinctively. The words I spoke were fuzzy, like someone had picked all the substance away from them, leaving only the bones. “We really did. What should we do with all this space? This place is so much bigger than any of the others!” Her sentences were malformed. Something had been ripped away from them. My head throbbed in rhythm with her voice. The signal was weak. This was all it could provide. “Maybe that room can be for you! Although I’m not really sure if you’d use it that much.” Tears started to form in my eyes. “I’m honestly not sure either. Maybe it could be for you?” My body felt stiff. This wasn’t the signal I was looking for. It was too muffled. “I don’t want to have to buy the equipment. Plus the membership—” That wasn’t what I said. Those words weren’t hers and these weren’t mine. Tears slid down my face. I couldn’t look at her anymore. She wasn’t there. The only thing that I could make out was her lips and that wasn’t enough. I needed all of her, but the radio wouldn’t allow it; it was too broken. The crackling static crashed in like tall waves. It got louder and louder.. The walls became fuzzy and speckled. The boxes were washed away with each thundering wave. I looked towards her but all I could see was static. It had devoured her. It filled my ears and my eyes and my head as it consumed me. This was the closest I had come to her. Maybe next time the signal would be right. Maybe I could see her again. I took a moment to hold my head until my mind reformed itself. The static left in a tide until it no longer occupied the crevasses of my skull. I noticed a small crack in the radio’s side. I ran my hand over the split in the metal, flakes of rust covering the pads of my fingers. Each broken signal left its mark on the radio. Eventually there would be nothing left. I kept turning the dial; the signal was close now. The voices between the frequencies felt clearer than before, like they had finally acknowledged me. They were trying to reach out. A chorus of voices surfaced from the hissing yet again, their words rippling through the static. “Okay… called… exactly… safe… home…” She was crouching in front of me while I sat on a chair, or maybe a stool. She was more tangible now, her silhouette encased in an angelic shimmer. A creature of light. We were in an office of some kind. The walls shifted from plaster to windows to brick. She held my hands in hers, her face turned upwards at me. “I’m so sorry.” Her voice was no longer just a member of the choir, she now lead it. “Here, hold out your hand really quick.” She kept saying things from before. This still wasn’t right, but she felt close. She wanted to connect, but the signal was weak. I gazed into her eyes, black, then brown, then green. They were shallow and unfamiliar, but I could still see the ocean within them. “I’m so glad you’re safe and okay.” There were shrouded figures all around us, concerned and scared. Creatures of dark. They whispered among themselves, their words indecipherable, their anxiety infectious. My heart pounded. I looked back to her, hoping to find comfort in her light. Her eyes were so clear, the irises navy blue. They glistening like sunlight through water. “Are you okay? They called me as soon as they could.” The other voices started to melt into hers. She was so clear, but the connection was too poor; there were parts of her that had been lost. “Yeah I’m alright. I don’t think it was a big deal but I guess they’re just being cautious.” Bits of my response had been omitted. My words were no longer fuzzy, but incomplete. “Better safe than sorry, right? I’m just glad you’re okay.” She looked at me with a mixture of concern and relief. She clasped my hands tightly. “Do you know what happened?” “Honestly I’m not totally sure. I was just trying to get some work done and then my brain just stopped working. I got confused and then just… scared. At least that’s what people told me. I don’t really remember.” My head was filled with holes. This was the best I could do. “That’s…” Her eyes glanced down at the floor. For a brief moment, they were oceans. My heart began to beat heavily again. The whispers among the figures grew louder. She raised her eyes back up to mine. “Do you want to head home now? Your boss gave me the okay for you to leave early.” Even with the holes in her words, she comforted me. “Yes please. I don’t feel super great.” I looked back at the figures as they conversed with each other. My head felt heavy. “It’s gonna be okay. I’ll always be here.” Light refracted off her eyes. “Thank you. I’ll always be here too.” The static flowed in again, but this time, it was a soft stream. It filled up the room until everything was washed away. I let it soak into me. I was close now. I would find the signal soon. I would be able to see her again. Tide pools in my head slowly drained of the static. The radio’s dial had cracked and split into pieces, leaving only the metal knob underneath. I pinched it between my forefinger and thumb and kept searching. The connection was the clearest it had been. Voices flew by, screaming at me, begging for attention. I stopped. It was her voice. No longer was it a conglomeration, but a singular, melodic tone. She was talking directly to me. I responded, unhindered. We sat on an old, rusted bench that overlooked a secluded beach. It was overcast and fog obscured anything distant. A cold wind knocked against us, forcing us to huddle together while we watched the ocean. I rested my head on her shoulder as she leaned into me. We listened to the sound of waves crashing upon hidden rocks beyond the fog. I broke the silence. “I’ve always loved when its foggy. Makes it feel like you’re in a dream. I hope it feels like this all the time.” She turned her head to me as I lifted mine from her shoulder. She was wearing coral pink lipstick, even though it was just the two of us. Her navy blue eyes looked into mine for a moment, then out towards the ocean. “I think I like it more when its sunny. It makes the entire beach seem alive. Plus the water looks pretty when the sun hits it. I like all the colors.” “Okay, but what about when its all rainy and gloomy like this, you could see a rainbow! Those have all the colors you need!” She let out a small laugh. “Okay true… but you do need sunlight for a rainbow.” “Oh, yeah. I kinda forgot about that. Well regardless, it’s always peaceful, just in different ways.” She smiled at me for a moment, then looked back to the ocean. “Why aren’t you scared?” Her tone was stern. I looked at the ocean too. “I am scared!” I said slightly forcefully. “I guess I just got it into my head somehow that it’ll be like a living dream. And sure, some times you’ll have a nightmare, but all the other times you’ll be in places like this!” I gestured with my head towards the sea, then looked back at her. She was deep in thought. “I hope it’s like that. I’m just worried that I’m going to lose you to those dreams. I’ve been worried about it since that day I picked you up from work.” She wasn’t sad, not visibly. Her eyes glanced downwards for a moment. “Hey! I made a promise to you that I’d always be here for you. I’m not about to break it.” My tone was lighthearted, but I meant it. “Yeah, I know. I made the same promise to you though, so I’m not about to break it either.” “Guess it’s solved then! Come on lets go see how cold the water is.” I stood up and looked for a good way to get down to the beach. I wanted her to stop thinking about it. “Hey, lets make another promise together.” She clasped my hand as I started to walk away. I turned back to her and met her eyes with mine. Light refracted off them in a way that made the moment feel unreal. “Lets promise each other that, even when we’re dreaming, we’ll always be there for each other. Okay?” Her voice shook a little. She was scared. I was too. “Okay. I promise.” “I love you.” “I love you too. Always.” I took her hand and tugged her down a trail that was concealed by tall stalks of grass. “I’m totally pushing you in.” “Like you could! I’m like ten times stronger than you.” “We’ll see about that.”

item.title: A History of the Soul and its Impact on Brazil-United States Relations
item.description: On March 13th, 2027, a group of military scientists at Bharathiar University in Coimbatore, India, discovered the existence of the soul. They were instructed to conceal their findings while continuing research into, what they labeled, “human essence”. This secret was held for three months and seventeen days, but soon the entire world knew the reality of the soul. A year later, in Basel, Switzerland, scientists working under Roche Molecular Diagnostics successfully achieved an electrical output from the soul of a brain-dead woman. They published their discovery, claiming that the total power extracted was equivalent to “the daily electrical consumption of 150 households”. However, in the process, the woman died. As more countries developed their own ways of collecting souls for energy, land disputes and small-scale conflicts in high population areas became increasingly common. World leaders focused on utilizing foreign souls to increase the quality of life within their nations. The first soul collection facility was opened on July 3rd, 2029, just outside Kano, Nigeria. The first “es-car” was created on October 27th, 2031, in San Diego. Spurred on by French and Italian territorial claims, conflict in the regions surrounding the Arabian sea began to increase throughout 2032. This led to a large-scale Euro-Asian unification movement, focused on stabilizing the global east. The campaign eventually spread across the entire northern hemisphere, accelerated by increased fear of global war. On June 14th, 2034, the “Essence Protection Treaty” (EsPT) was signed by 93 countries. Since then, conflict in the North has decreased exponentially. In the early months of 2041, Brazilian authorities made several announcements cementing their commitment to keep soul collection facilities nationalized. The recently elected president of the United States, Steven Price, subsequently called for a private meeting with his Secretary of Defense, Ryan Horne, to discuss U.S. influence in the region. “This is an act of humiliation,” were the first words out of the President’s mouth. “They think they can make a mockery out of America.” The white overhead lights in the conference room were chosen to complement his skin, but the red that currently filled his cheeks made them worthless. Horne reclined in the seat next to him, leaving the other 12 chairs around the table empty, and jotted down his thoughts in a black binder marked with the seal of the U.S. army. “Mr. President, it is becoming increasingly clear that Brazil’s actions pose an existential threat to the United States,” he said slowly, his tone similar to one that would be used to ridicule a child. The President did not notice, the words appearing calculated and sharp in his mind. “Horne, I’m going to ask you a question, and it’s going to effect this entire thing, okay?” He smirked as he spoke, projecting his voice to regain control of the exchange. Horne nodded his head slowly as he locked eyes with the President, wrestling the rising anxiety in his chest, subduing it into a warped sense of confidence; something he had decades of practice doing. “Of course, Mr. President. Ask away.” The President smiled at him and raised his eyebrows, proud of Horne’s initiative. Through this uncomfortable combination of facial expressions, Horne got a good look at the effects of time on the man’s face; his usually baggy skin pulled taught by the tired muscles underneath. He thought for a moment about his own appearance at that age, but assured himself that he would be handsome until death, and maybe even after. “How do you think this great nation can continue to not only survive, but be the best in the world, Horne? I know my answer,. I’ve given it a lot of thought.” The President continued to awkwardly smile at Horne, studying him while he considered the question. He thought about how Horne’s skin looked like it had been shrink-wrapped onto his skull, and how much he was balding at thirty-six. He thanked God that he stilled looked this handsome at sixty-eight. “As of right now, essence, Mr. President. The more we control, the taller we stand. Our great forefathers knew that coal and oil were the only way to take control of our destiny, and now we stand in the same position.” Horne congratulated himself on his answer with a smirk. The President’s grin shifted into a toothy smile, one that he had practiced tirelessly. “You’ve only got half of it Horne. Only half!” He said, followed by a raspy chuckle. Horne’s eyes widened slightly as the President spoke. “We need to assure the protection of the true patriots, those that deserve to live in these terrific states. We need to show that we cannot be shoved around and bullied. These guys down in Brazil, they need to be taught that you don’t mess with us, you don’t mess with America without repercussions.” The President wiped the film of sweat off his forehead with the cuff of his suit, staining it. Horne paused for a moment, letting the sound of the President’s slight wheezing fill the room. He glanced down at the notes he had taken earlier. “Make him agree” were the only words on the page. He turned back to the President, who gazed at him in a way that suggested his feelings were hurt. “You’re absolutely right, Mr. President. We need to make a show-of-force. The EsPT prevents us from direct action, of course, but we can work around that.” He lifted the top page in his binder, exposing a grocery list underneath. He pretended to read it, and paused for a moment to think. “If you give the order, we can do it, Steven. We can save and elevate our great nation’s reputation in one go, and with the added benefit of more access to essence farms.” He gave his best attempt at a smile of approval, weak as it was, to the President, who grinned widely back. The President shot out his hand, and was almost giddy when Horne shook it. “We’re doing God’s work, Horne.” Horne, hearing this, felt an almost renewed sense of patriotism. Maybe we really are, he thought. On April 24th, 2041, U.S. operatives contacted Brazilian military official Antônio Luciano de Sousa, known as Tonho, and convinced him to initiate a U.S. funded coup d’état. A month later, 12 Brazilian officials had been killed, and Tonho was appointed president. U.S. involvement in the coup was not made public, but President Price stated that it was “a fantastic and much needed change for the country,” and hoped that the U.S. and Brazil could now “see eye-to-eye on issues of the modern day.” In June of the same year, Tonho attended several meetings with Price, all held at the White House. On July 3rd, the U.S. Press Secretary announced the formation of a new committee that would work with Tonho’s administration to “assist with the oversight and privatization of Brazil’s essence industry.” Tonho announced to news outlets that it was “a new and unprecedented era for the economic future of Brazil,” and Price called it “a big blow to socialism and a victory for democracy” on his social media accounts. Large-scale protests erupted the next day throughout Brazil. The phrase “Uma Só Alma,” or “One Soul,” was used as a slogan, calling for the government to re-nationalize soul production. Brasília was used as a stage for the largest of the protests, with people bussing in from the surrounding areas in order to increase visibility. Tonho quickly deployed military police to try and quell the movement, calling it “an affront to the good people of Brazil.” This only served to escalate the conflict. A week later, a crowd of upwards of 10,000 people had gathered in Brasília. While there was no head orchestrator of the protest, several left-wing organizations based in and around the city made their presence known. One of these organizations, “União Revolucionária Futura,” or “Future Revolutionary Union,” consisting of a small band of people from the Cidade Ocidental region of Goiás, was one of the first groups to gather in front of the National Congress building on the morning of the protest. Marcos tugged on his balaclava, pulling the thin fabric into a position that made breathing easier. The mask made him claustrophobic, and his double layer of sweatshirts, heavy cargo pants, and overstuffed backpack only intensified the feeling. His comrades had carefully planned the outfits a week prior, making sure they covered everything but the eyes and provided a good amount of padding. Everything they wore was black except for the grungy second-hand bike helmets that each of them had strapped to their backpacks, to be used when the police came. Their group, União Revolucionária Futura, consisted of eleven people, but only nine of them were present. Rato couldn’t take the time off work and Riven was taking care of his grandmother. Marcos tensed as he thought about them not being there to help. He looked out at the looming gray towers of the congressional building; the muted hues of dawn behind them frightened him. “Curupira, how are feeling you right now?” Besouro, a member of the group that had only joined recently, walked over to him, positioning herself at his side. She had immigrated from the U.S. around a month ago, and was still working on her Portuguese. “I’m doing alright. A bit worried for later, I guess, when the cops show up.” When he talked his balaclava slipped into his mouth, soaking the loose fabric in saliva, making it hard to draw air. “Me too,” was all she said before turning her attention to the congressional building. She gripped a sign made from tattered cardboard that read “Souls are part of us. Humanity > Progress.” They sat in silence for a moment and stared at the building together; the slowly rising sun reflecting off the windows, hurting their eyes. She patted him on the back and then went to talk to someone else. Each time someone used his alias he would tense up and press his teeth together, even though he had picked it himself. He had gotten the name from an ugly cartoon painting of the Curupira on the outside of his pre-school. The painting had always scared him as a kid, and his dad would have to hold his hand whenever he went to school. A shiver went down his back, distracting him from the memory. He looked down at the grass in front of him, the well maintained lawn contrasting the gray street he stood on. A small piece of the asphalt had broken away and sunken into the grass. He picked it up, put it in his pocket, and went to join the members of the group in making signs, anxious for the crowds to form. After a few hours, Marcos was face-to-face with a police officer. His group had created a bubble, with him and two comrades at the front and the others in the back holding signs, ready to support them or swap positions if anything went wrong. The groups surrounding them were in similar formations, with the bravest of them up against the armored police. They held signs and banners that read “One Soul,” or “Give Us Back Our Souls,” or some variant of the two. Marcos was forced into the officer in front of him by the weight of the crowd, the only separation between the two being a transparent riot shield. “You took everything from me! You took everything I had! I will make you pay!” he repeated, screaming at the officer at the top of his lungs as small bubbles of spit formed on the surface of his mask. Marcos felt absent in the moment; he focused on the eyes of the officer, hidden behind the glossy finish of the shield and a protective riot helmet. The man looked angry, the veins near his temples bulging from under his skin, pounding in rhythm with his heart. He didn’t know what the state had done. He didn’t know Marcos’ father, what a great man he was. He didn’t know what a cancer diagnosis meant in the country, how it’s easier to sell yourself than waste away. He didn’t know what it felt like to open a check for a sum that could barely pay for the funeral. Or maybe he did. Either way, in that moment, it was entirely his fault. Marcos reached into his pocket, took out the piece of asphalt, and started to smash it against the officer’s head. Each time he forced the rock down, it would glide off the helmet, leaving a streak of ashy black. The officer, after a moment of shock, backed up while Marcos continued to hit him. Marcos knew what was coming, but the crowd behind him pushed against him fiercely, and his comrades weren’t there to help, as they were distracted by the other police in the line. Two officers filled in the other’s position, grabbed Marcos, and threw him towards them. He pounded at them desperately, the asphalt shedding pieces with each strike to their heads, until it crumbled in his hand. Just as Marcos was about to cross beyond the line of police, he felt a force behind him, desperately pulling on his backpack in an attempt to wrench him back into the crowd. His balance faltered due to the polar forces, causing him to partially fall backwards, leaving his legs on the ground but his body held upright by the tugging of his backpack. He felt like a wounded soldier being carried across a battlefield. The police were now pulling on his legs, so he began to kick them, making sure to aim for their heads. He was finally able to conjure enough force to deliver a firm blow to one of the officers, causing him to fall backwards, the visor on his helmet breaking in the process. Marcos was dragged into the crowd as he whooped and yelled victoriously, his position quickly being replaced by one of his comrades. A clearing had been formed around him, allowing him to pick himself up. He brushed off the dirt and dust on his pants, feeling a rip in the fabric near his calf, and looked up expecting to see a member of his group. A woman without a mask, without black clothing or a helmet, stared back at him. “Are you okay?” she yelled, the noise of the crowd muffling her words. “I’m okay. Thank you. I would have been arrested if you hadn’t dragged me away,” Marcos shouted, baffled that the women did such a thing. She surveyed Marcos as if she was making sure that he was actually okay. “What’s your name?” she asked, moving closer to Marcos so he could hear her better. “Curupira.” On the 16th of July, a CIA whistle blower sent documents to major news outlets detailing America’s involvement in the coup that placed Tonho in power. In response, “One Soul” protests erupted throughout the U.S. in solidarity with Brazil. These protests lasted until the 22nt of July, ending when Tonho announced a social program that would return a large percentage of the profits from private soul production to the people of Brazil. Six months later, Tonho quietly released a memo, stating that the social program would be placed in the control of the United States Brazilian Essence Security Committee. The day after, the CIA whistle blower was found dead in a hotel room in Columbus, Ohio, in an apparent suicide. Small groups, including those that were present at the larger “One Soul” protests, continue to grow in size due to this decision, but struggle to find influence over the Brazilian government. The “Future Revolutionary Union,” however, has been attempting to form a coalition between several of these organizations in an effort to gain wider political power. This has elevated their influence throughout the regions surrounding Brasília, but many collectives still refuse to join, questioning if “the union truly believes in the revolutionary politics, or if it’s just a part of their name.” Yearly global soul production is expected to rise to 150 million by 2050, with Brazil contributing 20 million, or roughly 13%. Brazil and the U.S. remain close allies since the formation of Tonho’s government.

item.title: Backwood Despondence
item.description: The theater was small and cramped. There were only about twenty chairs in the room, and most of them were filled. Two small chandeliers hung low from the ceiling, giving me just enough light to navigate to the last available seat in the back row. The other people in the aisle squeezed against their chairs as I pushed by. It was my second or third time at The Higher Depths—I couldn’t recall if I had seen The American Clock here or at Carpenter Square a few seasons ago—but I had yet to be impressed with its productions. The theater’s insistence on hosting inexperienced writers and directors yielded plays that disrespected the medium as a whole. I had been writing theater reviews in the Oklahoma Times for about 10 years, and this show had been getting buzz in the local papers, so I was forced to attend against my better judgment. I held a notepad in my lap—I never understood how people could get through a play without a notepad, how else would one keep track of their thoughts?—and looked around at the other people in the audience. It seemed to be a split between droopy-eyed elders and blue-collar twenty-somethings. I sighed through my nose while scribbling down a note. Audience is who you’d expect.
